newsitem.title: UK: Ad giant WPP profits up 35 percent.
newsitem.headline: Ad giant WPP profits up 35 percent.

text.p: WPP, the world's largest advertising and marketing services group, Wednesday reported a 35 percent jump in 1996 profits to 153 million pounds ($246 million) and said it hoped to be debt-free in two years.

However, WPP shares slid 14p (22.5 cents) to 253p ($4.06) on disappointment that the company, which owns giant advertising agencies J. Walter Thompson and Ogilvy & Mather, did not announce a share buy-back as expected.
WPP said it earmarked 25 million pounds ($40.1 million) for buy-backs but said these would take place when "market conditions are appropriate."
"There is no particular timing for this. We think there may be a time when the best investment may be in the company's stock," Chief Executive Martin Sorrell told Reuters.
The profits were at the top end of market forecasts but analysts said WPP shares eased after adding almost 10 percent over the past week on hopes of a buy-back.
Sorrell will shortly be awarded shares worth at least 2.7 million pounds ($4.3 million) if the WPP share price continues above 230p ($3.70).

As part of a special rewards package, Sorrell is entitled to 1.17 million shares if the price remains above that 230p trigger level for 60 working days. It passed that point in late December and the shares could be awarded in mid-March.
WPP almost collapsed under the weight of its debt early in this decade after acquiring its two main advertising agencies in the late 1980s.
But it cut its average debt from 214 million to 145 million pounds ($343.7 million to $232.9 million) in 1996 and said debt could be eliminated in aboutu two years.

WPP generated 41 percent of its revenue in North America, 20 percent in continental Europe and 19 percent in Britain. The remainder came from Asia Pacific, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East combined.
